text:
Predicates:
Nemesis(x, y) ::: x is the nemesis of y.
Wins(x, y) ::: x wins against y.
AppearsIn(x, y) ::: x appears in y.
NamedAfter(x, y) ::: x is named after y.
GoodGuys(x) ::: x are the good guys.
Fight(x, y) ::: x fights y.
Movie(y) ::: y is a movie.
Character(y) ::: y is a character.
Name(y, x) ::: y is named after x.
---

Premises:
∀x (Movie(x) → ∃y (Character(y) ∧ Name(y, x))) ::: If a movie is a superhero movie, it is named after a character.
NamedAfter(surprisingAdventures, sirDigby) ::: The Surprising Adventures of Sir Digby Chicken Caesar is named after Sir Digby.
In superhero movies, the good guys always win.
GoodGuys(x) → ∀y (Fight(x, y) → Wins(x, y))
SirDigbyFightsNemesis ::: Sir Digby fights his nemesis.
∀x (Fight(sirDigby, x) → Nemesis(x, sirDigby))
If somebody wins a fight, the person they are fighting loses.
∀x ∀y (Fight(x, y) ∧ Wins(x, y) → ¬Wins(y, x))
If a superhero movie is named after a character, that character appears in the movie.
NamedAfter(x, y) → AppearsIn(y, x)
---

Conclusion:
AppearsIn(nemesis, surprisingAdventures) ::: The nemesis of Sir Digby appears in the movie.
Since Sir Digby fights his nemesis and good guys always win, Sir Digby's nemesis loses.
Therefore, the statement "Sir Digby’s nemesis loses" is true.
